utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6335, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you've seen this before as well, sir. This is a video of the 10th Sabotage Detachment celebration at Vlasenica in October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to 10 minutes, 50 seconds to make it -- oh, we're there. We can play.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember being at that celebration?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR KOSORIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to 00:13:32.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, if we could go back to that. Okay. We're at 00:13:36.6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You correct me if I am wrong. We see here you, Vujadin Popovic, and General Krstic at this 10th Sabotage celebration; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to identify the persons in the still rather than Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is cross-examination and I may lead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that's you, Popovic, and Krstic at the 10th Sab celebration?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR KOSORIC
utterances.text: I see myself here, I see Krstic, but I don't see Popovic. The tall, strong guy is the Chief of Staff of the Sehovac brigade. I don't see Popovic here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's play it some more. [Video-clip played].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who is that on the right? We're at 13:39.9.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR KOSORIC
utterances.text: The one with his hands crossed. That's Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's play this another second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's a bit blurry at the moment but that's you next to Popovic; right? And we're at 13:41.9.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR KOSORIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this is October 1995. This is even by your testimony today after you know about the murders from the international community. You're with Krstic and Popovic at the 10th Sab celebration. Didn't you know at this time that, one, that the 10th Sabotage had taken part in mass executions, two -- well, I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR KOSORIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you know in October 1995 from international organisations and others that the 10th Sabotage Unit had taken part in mass executions at Branjevo Farm?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR KOSORIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember. I was there, but when exactly I found out, it was in the autumn, but I had nothing to do with the 10th Sabotage Detachment. It's a Main Staff unit. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's start with the most recent things. Within whose remit is the investigation into crimes or illegal behaviour of our own soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR KOSORIC
utterances.text: This is done by our security service and the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that in the remit of your service?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR KOSORIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do make a short pause before answering, please. Did you see a document anywhere saying that there was illegal killing in Podrinje in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR KOSORIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that Mr. Nicholls corrected that mistake, but let us check anyway. Do you distinguish between entourage and escort?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR KOSORIC
utterances.text: Escort something else. He had his own escort, and his entourage included everybody -- all of us, all who had come from the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant-Colonel, do you distinguish between killed meaning murdered and killed like killed in the battle-field?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR KOSORIC
utterances.text: Who -- someone was killed if they -- if there was -- if that person was shot, executed, whereas killed in action is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the words of General Mladic quoted to you on page 10, the words that he said to the Muslims, did you conclude that anybody would be illegally killed?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR KOSORIC
utterances.text: No. I couldn't believe that, because he is a professional military officer. It is clear who can decide that someone should be killed. It's only a court. And whoever was ordered to kill these people should have refused orders. That's what I would have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did anybody or anything warn you of illegal killings in the coming days?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR KOSORIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel, for your testimony and for coming here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, unless my colleagues have a question for you, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're waiting for the next witness, I could maybe just advise you there are a couple of associated exhibits that we're not offering. Would you be inclined to take that up now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Prosecution pointed out to us correctly that there were two duplicates, so 1D7890 and 1D7891 will not be offered. In addition, there were seven documents that were not translated and as a result we won't be offering those documents. And there are eight documents that are partially translated and we're only offering those portions which are translated, and we will conform the B/C/S to the English translation so that only those portions which are translated will be in the B/C/S in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a short break, five minutes? Yes. --- Break taken at 11.45 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, could you give us the exhibit -- or 65 ter numbers of those exhibits that you are tendering only parts of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, 1D07856, 05985, 059 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. 5985 means 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about 1D7857? I'm -- I'm referring to those exhibits that was referred to by the witness only in part, whether we should admit only those parts discussed or in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think the witness actually refers to all of the exhibits only in part to some extent, so we haven't in the past been that selective when witnesses have referred to documents, but I would say that we should admit the entire document except for those which we haven't provided translations. This was a decision we made to do partial translations because of the time that we had between the time we had the statement and the time that the witness was going to testify. We didn't think that the language section would have time to translate the entire documents so we tried to make their work easier. But in principle, for documents where there is a full translation, we would like the entire document to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It has been the Chamber's practice and the Chamber is minded to follow that, which practice is that we have been admitting only those parts dealt with unless there's some good cause to admit it in its entirety. So what about 1D7857 that was dealt with in paragraph 28? Can I hear from you, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Most of these documents are government sessions from the time period when the witness was the prime minister. I certainly see Your Honour's desire to limit the evidence to what the witness discussed. On the other hand, the witness was the prime minister. These are the government minutes. It's -- you know, we have no problem with the entire document going in, and we're in Your Honours' hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if the Prosecution is okay with following the Chamber's practice, we'll admit only the cover page and the portions referred to. And the same applies to 1D7876. So we'll admit only cover page and item 20. And 1D7886 -- no. Strike that. 65 ter number -- no, strike it again. Yes, that's it. And the Chamber finds the following items, the documents, not forming an inseparable and indispensable part of the statement and thereby will not admit them as associated exhibits. They are as follows: 1D7851, referred to in para 20; 1D7880, referred to in para 74; 1D7884, referred to in para 81; 65 ter number 18073, in para 81; 21652, referred to in paragraph 34; and 26196, referred to in paragraph 31. The statement can be understood without those documents. So having dealt with that issue, we'll bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one point, and that is that 1D7876 that you indicated you would just be admitting in part is actually one of those that we don't have a translation for. So we wouldn't be tendering that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, thank you. Thank you. Probably I missed that. Thank you for your notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm also having trouble finding 26196. I'm wondering if that's admitted as -- is that -- you were referring then to 1D26196, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll come back to that later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Lukic, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule that we have here at the Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E) of Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Professor Lukic.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: The Defence team. Yes. You mean this Defence team. Yes. It's about 28 pages long.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D7850, please. 1D7850. That is the proper number as recorded. Something seems wrong with e-court. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you see that statement of yours on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I remind both you and myself not only to speak slowly but also to make a pause between question and answer. Did you read and sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I read this statement and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us show the last page for Professor Lukic to identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I think I wasn't able to relate to you everything I know and everything I experienced, but what is shown here is my full statement and I believe that includes all essential things in connection with the events in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions today that were put to you by my collaborators, would your answers be essentially the same as in this statement?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: They would certainly be the same, because I read and signed this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I tender this 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Having heard this morning that the -- that there are seven documents discussed in the statement that will not be tendered due to the lack of translation, the witness's discussion and comments on those documents should be redacted from the statement given that the documents are no longer being offered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does the statement stand alone? It cannot be understood without the documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, the parts where these documents are discussed I think not. For example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For example -- could you give me an example.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: An example would be paragraph 26, which discusses 1D07855, and it says: "It can be seen from item 18 that there were problems in the judiciary for a number of reasons." But that document and item 18 are not being tendered, so it's difficult to understand what the witness is speaking about without the underlying document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One more example.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: For example, paragraph 59 dealing with 1D7873. "As can be seen from this document," this is in the middle of the paragraph, "I continued to strive for the Executive Committee and Assembly and every municipality had to take up their functions completely." Again we don't have the document, so the comment "as can be seen from the document" doesn't work there. The underlying document is not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we disagree, and we think that the witness's comments can be understood without reference to these documents. The Prosecution has the documents translated now. They received copies last night. The cross-examination will be continuing. If they feel there's something that they want to explore about the document they can do that, but we believe that this -- it would be unfair to redact the passage where the witness gives substantive information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, the Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson's view, and the Chamber is of the view that the statement could be understood without the document itself, and if necessary, you can take up the issue in your cross-examination. And as to the item you indicated, pointed out, Mr. Robinson, you were correct, and I meant 1D26196.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I also neglected to ask that these documents be added to our Rule 65 ter list because we didn't -- hadn't interviewed the witness at the time that that list was filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No objection from you, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit the statement as well the associated exhibits as we have dealt with so far. Now, shall we give the -- assign the exhibit number for the statement at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will be Exhibit D3563. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And all the remaining documents will be assigned exhibit number by the Registrar in due course. Please proceed, continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd now like to read out the summary of Professor Lukic's statement in English. [In English] Vladimir Lukic was born on the 7th of April, 1933, in Dabar, Sanski Most municipality. In early June 1992, Radovan Karadzic appointed him commissioner for the municipality of Novo Sarajevo. From July the 1st until 19th of December, 1992, Vladimir Lukic worked as the representative of the Republika Srpska at the UNPROFOR in Sarajevo. Vladimir Lukic received many reports about crimes against Serbs in Sarajevo. He passed on all reports and eyewitness accounts to the UNPROFOR but did not receive satisfactory responses. Vladimir Lukic found UNPROFOR to be negatively disposed towards the Serbian side in a number of respects. UNPROFOR was inconsistent in enforcing the ban on firing from its immediate vicinity. It was further always assumed without checking that shelling was committed by Serbs. Vladimir Lukic believed that the sniping in Sarajevo was started by the Muslim side and that UNPROFOR was aware of the Muslim snipers in Sarajevo. He observed that when Serbian artillery fired at a target in the city, it was always a military target, although UNPROFOR would nonetheless described it as a civilian target. There was no organised shelling of civilians by Serbs in Sarajevo. The only possibility was that there were individual incidents of retaliation that were outside of normal system of command. In mid-December 1992, Vladimir Lukic was approached by Radovan Karadzic to be prime minister of the new government and accepted. Throughout his prime ministership, Vladimir Lukic had no problems with Radovan Karadzic, with regard to his independence and the independence of the government. The position of the government was that all citizens of the RS, regardless of ethnicity, must be guaranteed freedom of movement according to their freely expressed will. This government position had been absolute support -- had the absolute support of Radovan Karadzic. The government constantly called for the establishment of the rule of law and the protection of all citizens including refugees regardless of ethnicity. This included ordering the ministries of interior and defence and the security service of the VRS to use all legal means to protect civilians and their property regardless of ethnicity. The electricity situation in Republika Srpska was dramatically bad, which affected all sides of society. The Muslim side repeatedly cut power supply lines. The government discussed taking reciprocal measures to prevent this but decided against it because the civilian population under Muslim control would suffer as a result. That was Government of Republika Srpska. The Government of Republika Srpska called for the unhindered passage of humanitarian convoys to both Muslims and Croats again with the absolute support of Radovan Karadzic. The government tried with all its powers to prevent private and illegal relocation of refugees and demanded that criminal proceedings be initiated against those who were involved in such activities. Similarly, when Vladimir Lukic heard of incidents of looting of civilian convoys, he called for investigation and for the perpetrators to be punished. The government generally called for everyone who had committed crimes to answer for their actions regardless of the ethnicity of the perpetrator. When the -- Vladimir Lukic and his colleagues, including Radovan Karadzic, received a report that certain judges were being threatened in cases that were being conducted against Serbs, they concluded that the safety in work of these judges should be guaranteed. The government experienced significant problems with the municipalities which functioned as states within a state with significant power. The Presidency and the government fought to centralise government in keeping with the constitution and reduce the autonomous behaviour of municipalities which adopted regulations which conflicted with the laws. And that would be short summary, and at that moment I don't have additional questions to Professor Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in its entirety in writing, that is, through your written witness statement, and now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Dr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At paragraph 4 of your statement, you explain that you were the Republika Srpska representative at UNPROFOR stationed in the PTT building in Sarajevo. Who appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I was appointed to that position by the President of Republika Srpska, Mr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you were a representative of the civilian Republika Srpska authorities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did you report to Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I reported to Dr. Karadzic above all others, but since communications weren't operational at all time -- at all times, we weren't able to be in contact. I reported to other persons such as vice-presidents to Karadzic, Professor Koljevic, Ms. Plavsic, and some other individuals whom I knew and who were interested in the issues that I was dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And in your statement you said that while you were in that position you received up to several hundred visitors daily of people living in Sarajevo. Were those mainly ethnic Serbs who came to visit you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Most of them were Serbs, yes. However, there were all other ethnicities there, Jews, Muslims, Croats, et cetera. Many of them asked that I provide them with some sort of assistance, but most of them actually wanted to leave Sarajevo. You know that there were ways of going out, of leaving Sarajevo, but for the Serbs and Montenegrins, it was difficult to leave Sarajevo unless some additional measures were applied.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Lukic, given that my time is limited, I'd like to ask you to focus on the specific question I ask and try to limit your answer to just that question. And what were your tasks in relation to UNPROFOR when you were stationed at the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any assignments from UNPROFOR directly. However, they frequently asked that I help -- that we help the population receive water and power supplies and all other bare necessities. Especially when it came to humanitarian aid, we were to make sure that the aid reach the specific points that we had agreed upon with UNPROFOR. I also have to say this: When I arrived at Pale, I told Dr. Karadzic, or, rather, President Karadzic, what it was that I had been doing. I would particularly speak to him about the problems related to water, electricity, and humanitarian aid. He told me resolutely we do not have any intention of waging a war with humanitarian aid, water, or electricity that all citizens need as a bare necessity.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when you were working in the PTT building, were you still living in Grbavica and travelling back and forth, or did you stay -- or did you live somewhere inside the city?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: No. Those of us who were delegated to UNPROFOR lived there and went home only for personal needs.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you lived and worked in the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had our own offices where we slept.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And how often, if ever, would you travel around the Muslim-held parts of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: It was only on a couple of occasions that I did that when an officer of the English army made two mistakes. Instead of going to Lukavica, he actually missed a turn and drove us around town. So that was the only time when I actually was able to observe the town, save for the occasions when I would be going home, that's to say, Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And I think's clear from your prior answer, but if you could just make it absolutely clear. It was not part of your job to carry out any investigations into any shelling or sniping incidents in Sarajevo, was it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, because I could not have been there without observing what was being shelled where, on the one hand, and on the other, I spent 37 years in Sarajevo altogether, what with schooling and my job. So I knew Sarajevo very well, and I intervened on several occasions that the Muslim forces should not be shelling in front of UNPROFOR, in front of the wire factory which was several metres away from UNPROFOR, in front of the civil engineering factory where I worked. And let me not enumerate all those places. At least a dozen more sites that the Muslim forces shelled and the shelling was quite often random because they would fire from rather small lorries. They were mortars, you see. And you can imagine how one would fire when one would actually just stop in a position quickly, launch a projectile and then move away fast, and normally these would be sites where it was not allowed to fire from.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, in your earlier answer you made clear that you lived and worked in the PTT building. You were only actually able to observe the town maybe twice when someone took a wrong turn on your way back to Lukavica. So it's clear, is it not, that the only observations you could make, personal observations you could make, would be observations of what was happening in and around the PTT building and perhaps something you may have seen on your way back to Lukavica; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: No. That is not the case, because certain points such as Vraca, which I crossed for -- which I crossed countless times, I was able to see all these various sites that I mentioned, and everything that happened close to UNPROFOR I was able to observe. Therefore it wasn't difficult for me to see what was going on because I knew the town pretty well. I was able to see more of the town as I was crossing Vraca than if I went to the railway station with an UNPROFOR officer, if I went to Marin Dvor and back. Then there was another occasion I went to Vase Miskina Crni and then again back in the direction of the PTT engineering, that is to say, in the direction of Lukavica. In other words, whoever wanted to look, could not fail to see Sarajevo. And of course, all of what I was referring to one could see with the naked eye, let alone with some sort of device if you had one.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I note the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm informed by the VWS only now that you had some concerns that you had to stay over the weekend at The Hague. Given the time for cross-examination, it seems evident that we cannot conclude your evidence today. I take it that is the case, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And next week we'll resume on Tuesday, but I'm confident we can conclude your evidence by Tuesday next week. Will it be okay with you, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that is what the Defence needs, I will stay, although I do have certain reasons why I would have to actually leave tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I appreciate your kind understanding. Thank you. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 23 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. -- Dr. Lukic, in your statement at paragraphs 11 and 12, you identified four locations in Sarajevo as locations where the Muslim side would fire artillery or mortars. That was near the UNPROFOR or PTT building, in front of the wire factory, the civil engineering faculty, and the tunnel above the civil engineering faculty. That tunnel you're referring to, that's the Ciglana tunnel, I take it; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: No. That was the tunnel leading to the hospital. Am I supposed to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Lukic. Are you talking about the state hospital? There's no tunnel leading to the state hospital; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: There is, above the faculty of construction, and the tunnel leads not to the main entrance, the south entrance. It's just above the civil engineering school. That's where one of the entrances into the hospital is. This is where our opponents hid weapons. They opened fire from there, and then they would quickly hide in the tunnel. Whoever left the hospital could not avoid traipsing over the weapons. Another thing, you said that I mentioned only four locations. I only mentioned four locations because I didn't think it necessary to mention another ten from which fire was opened from Sarajevo on our positions, but not only on our positions but also on our settlements around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. This tunnel you're talking about, is it a tunnel for vehicle traffic or is it a pedestrian tunnel?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Both. There are two tunnels. I believe that are -- confusing the two. One tunnel passes above the bypass, above the brickworks, and leads to that railway station. This is also a tunnel, and fire was opened from it on both sides. There is another tunnel, the tunnel that I've just referred to, at the entrance into the state hospital right below the surgical department, or at least the surgical department is very near. You know I worked at the school of civil engineering which is below that tunnel, below the road to -- to which the tunnel exits.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 15 of your statement you said: "I saw myself on many occasions when the Serbian artillery fired at a target in the city and this was always a military target." Can you please identify for me all the objects in Sarajevo where you saw with your own eyes Serbian artillery hit?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Our artillery opened fire on several locations that I saw. Firstly they opened fire on our opponents' artillery around those two tunnels. They also opened fire on the artillery below Buca Potok. They also opened fire on artillery positions near Standard, as well as the artillery that fired from behind the buildings at Marin Dvor, also the artillery that opened fire at us from the building of the Novo Sarajevo municipality or near that building, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And on any of those occasions, did the artillery shells hit their target or did you ever see those shells hit a civilian object?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I must say that I do not remember any shells that fell directly on civilian facilities, but I remember shells that fell close to civilian facilities, especially once the Serbian artillery was moved at a distance of 20 kilometres, which was its ultimate range, the ultimate range of the artillery, it could no longer be very precise. So the dispersion of such mortar shells is a well-known phenomenon in artillery. If I had ridden -- written, which I didn't do because I did not feel a need to record every direct hit, I would be able to tell you that I'm sure that there were direct hits on a civilian facility here and there. I was trained as an artillery officer, as a reserve artillery officer in land -- in the land army, and I know how shells scatters -- scatter on the ground. And I know that there's no artilleryman who can make a direct hits in the fashion of a sniper. It's just impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic, I asked you a very simple question about what you saw, and then you went into a long answer about principles of artillery. I just don't have sufficient time for you to answer my questions in such a manner, and I'd like to ask you again to focus on the questions that I ask. Now, you have said that the only possibility that you would allow in connection with alleged Serbian shelling of Sarajevo was that there were individual incidents of retaliation outside the normal system of command. So I take it your position is that there are only two possibilities, the Serb side was either firing at a military target or there were individual acts of retaliation. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, I should say that as a rule our artillery targeted military targets. I have no doubts about that. At the end of the day this can be confirmed by the number of facilities which were not targeted, although Serbian targets had been targeted from there. Buca Potok was targeted because there was the enemy artillery there, and they opened fire on us from there. I saw shells that pounded Buca Potok because there were several artillery assets there from which fire had been opened on us. Whether a house was hit or not, I don't know, but there probably were. But I know of a case when our civilian or a young guy came to tell us that his family had been chased out from their apartment in Kosevo Brdo, and he asked our artilleryman to open fire on his former apartment. This artilleryman didn't want to do that, but I wonder whether every artilleryman refused such a request. I suppose not. On the other hand, there is no artillery that will hit all the targets without hitting something else in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 11076, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic, this is an UNPROFOR damage assessment of the citizens hospital sent to the senior military observer in Sarajevo, and it's copied to Dr. Bakir Nakas, the citizens hospital director, and we know Dr. Nakas was the director of the state hospital. This is in English, so I will read the relevant parts to you. The damage assessment was conducted on the 31st of December, 1992, so just after you finished your stint in Sarajevo. And if we could go to page 3, at the bottom of the first paragraph it says: "Although not exhaustive due to quantity of AAA," which I believe refers to anti-aircraft fire, "and small arms, the following major impacts have occurred on the main building south side: "4th floor, one tank round which destroyed the burns operating theatre. "5th floor, three artillery or tank rounds. "6th floor, one 122-millimetre artillery plus multiple 20-millimetre anti-aircraft. "7th floor, one tank round and multiple 20-millimetre anti-aircraft. "8th floor, multiple 20-millimetre anti-aircraft. "9th floor, three tank rounds with a well-aimed 5 metre spacing. "10th floor, one 155-millimetre artillery and multiple 20-millimetre anti-aircraft." And on the next page at the top it describes damage to the annex building. It talks about multiple impacts from anti-aircraft and heavy machine-gun fire. And it says: "The northern side has received two 122-millimetre artillery impacts and the roof has sustained damage by a 128-millimetre rocket from a multiple-launch rocket system." Now, Dr. Lukic, do you consider the state hospital to be a military target, or is all of -- all of this fire the result of individual acts of retaliation?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I have my doubts about that report. I have my reasons for that. I received seven to ten doctors who worked at the state hospital. One of them was one of the chief plastic surgeons and so on and so forth. Therefore, I'm not saying that a shell didn't fall on the hospital. Nobody can claim that. However, for so many shells to have landed on the hospital, I can't accept that. I saw those doctors who informed me, obviously they didn't inform me about every single shell. However, if -- I absolutely do not agree with such a massive shelling of the hospital. Let me not mention the names of those doctors. I'd rather not do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6336, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just before we move on to the next topic, Dr. Lukic, I'm just going to ask you about one specific shelling incident that the Chamber heard evidence about, which is from the 12th of July, 19 -- sorry, I'm not -- my apologies, that's not from your time. I'll just move on. Now, at paragraph 27 of your statement you talked about your function as prime minister, and you said: "I never had problems with Dr. Karadzic with regard to my independence or the independence of the government." And at paragraph 33, you refer to item 45 of P3129.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could call that up, please. And this is an extract from the March -- 20th of March, 1993, government session which established a five-member government personnel commission. And this is on page 12 of the English and 17 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you can see under item 45, a five-member personnel commission was established and the fifth member is a representative of the SDS Main Board. And in your statement you said it was logical that easily the biggest party should have its representative in the personnel commission of the RS government. What was the reaction of the SDS party to the government creating its own personnel commission and providing for SDS representation on it? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I absolutely remember that. I don't see anything illogical in that. The president of the commission was my vice-president, the second member of the commission was my second vice-president, and my third minister was the third member, my fourth minister, and the minister of the interior was also a member. And it was only logical for the biggest party which rose to defend its people, which organised its people, had one of the party men as members. The same thing happens today. It's still a custom in our parts even today, so I don't see anything unusual or illogical there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Dr. Lukic. That wasn't my question. My question was about the reaction of the SDS to the government setting up this commission. How did the SDS react when you informed them that you had established this commission and that they were welcome to have a representative in that commission? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I remember, but I don't remember any reactions. Nothing special happened that I could highlight today. Let me see who attended the session. Can we go one page back, or can you show me the part where the attendees were recorded?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic, this is an associated exhibit in your statement. I'm not asking you about this session. I'm asking you about the SDS's reaction, so I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 18011, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you said you don't recall any reaction and "nothing special happened that I could highlight today." Well, here is a letter from the chairman of the SDS Executive Committee from the 12th of April, 1993, so a few weeks after the session we just looked at. It's addressed to you. And the subject is: "Reply to the information re the establishment of the government personnel commission." And it refers to a letter sent by you informing the SDS about the establishment of the commission and asking for one representative of the Main Board to join it. And then it says: "Regarding the increasing number of attempts to deny the undeniable political facts and taking unauthorised authorisations on all levels of conducting the policy, we feel obligated to inform you and warn you about the established rules of political conduct." And then under number 1, it refers to the SDS being the party in power. Under number 2, it notes that the National Assembly is 7/8ths SDS representatives, and your government has been voted and elected by the SDS deputies. And then it says: "You ought to be the government of the Serbian Democratic Party and you are the executive authority of the Assembly with the majority of seats of the Serbian Democratic Party, you implement the policy of that party." And number 4, which is the next page, it says: "As the party in power, we conduct the personnel policy, and without the personnel commission of the party on all levels from the municipality to the republic, no appointments will be possible without our approval." And under number 5: "I am not disputing that the government is thinking about improving the personnel policy, but I am disputing that it can have a commission which would appoint, verify, and discharge or give approvals. That is why we shall not send our member to your commission, because you ought to be our government and appoint our personnel for whom the approval will be given by the Serbian Democratic Party." Now, the SDS party was, in fact, incensed at your efforts to create a personnel commission because, as this letter states, the SDS is the party in power. It conducts the personnel policy, and it is the task of the government to implement that policy; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I must admit that you have jogged my memory and reminded me of something that we at the government didn't agree. All the government members were members of the SDS, so I -- I thought then and I still think that a government that is elected by the Assembly is entitled to dealing with certain issues, especially when it comes to its own purview of work, but it is also true that there were some members of the Executive Council and Executive Board that thought differently. But I must say that in conversations with Dr. Karadzic, all that was ironed out, and it was all reduced to a normal situation. There were no grave accusations as one might conclude from reading this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, whether or not there were any grave accusations, the government, after receiving this letter, did change its approach and deferred to the SDS on personnel matters and sought SDS approval of personnel matters, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Not always.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we go to 65 ter 18012, and I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6337, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, this is a letter from the government secretary, Mr. Lakic, to the Executive Committee of the SDS, dated the 29th of August, 1993, and it asks for the SDS's opinion regarding the staff nominated to the positions within state organs, public enterprises, and enterprises of particular significance for the republic. And then it lists a number of proposals, 1 to 18. And on the next page under numbers 19 to 21, it seeks proposals from the SDS for certain management boards. And if we could go now to the response, which is 65 ter 18013. This is the response from the SDS, dated the 28th of December, 1993, signed by Dr. Karadzic, and the subject is: "Approval of appointments," and it refers to this previous letter and says: "We hereby inform you that the Serbian Democratic Party personnel commission approves," and then there are two approvals for two people, and then it instructs which -- that six people shall be appointed members of the pension and disability fund administrative board. Now, this exchange of letters shows, Dr. Lukic, that the government can propose candidates for functions in state organs and public enterprises, but it is the SDS that ultimately decides; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: That is indeed so if you take it that President Karadzic is functioning completely in the service of the government rather than in the service of the president of the republic. His role as the president of the republic is, of course, the highest when it comes to the personnel. Now, regardless of whether the proposing party is the government or the SDS board.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, the header on this letter is the RS Serbian Democratic Party. The -- it's -- Dr. Karadzic states that the approval has been given by the personnel commission, and it is stamped with the Serbian Democratic Party stamp. So this letter from Dr. Karadzic is a reflection of approval at the highest -- from the highest levels of the SDS party, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Certainly. President Karadzic is president of the SDS and President of Republika Srpska, and that is absolutely the highest level. I have to say there were never any disagreements, at least not significant ones, when it came to the president of the republic. In the majority of the cases, he gave his approval to our proposals.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 18014, and I would tender those two documents we just looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Two documents. We admitted the previous one. Yes. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There was one we admitted and then there was this exchange of letters that we've just looked at, so there are two more. They're 18012 and 18013.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President. I note that the English translation of this 18013 is showing up as access denied on our e-court, but hopefully it will be fixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm informed it should be released now, and our apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit them. Shall we give the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibits P6338 and P6339, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could have 65 ter 18014.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is a letter from March 1994 from the -- your chef de cabinet, Zdravko Miovcic to the president of the SDS Executive Board and there are some preliminaries, and then it says: "We suggest that SDS personnel board considers the possibility of issuing the approval for Radivoje Pandurevic to carry out the duties of assistant minister of finance." Now, here your office is asking permission from the SDS personnel board to appoint this individual to the position of assistant minister of finance; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6340, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to P1379 now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is the 34th Republika Srpska Assembly session, and it's referenced in your statement at paragraph 62, and that's where you refer to a speech by Dr. Karadzic where he talks about not having the prime minister in his pocket, and you refer to this as an example of your independence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 168 of the English and 175 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You don't mention anywhere in your statement what you said at this session, Dr. Lukic, so I'd like to ask you a question or two about that. And this is at the bottom of the B/C/S and the top of the English. This is Mirko Mijatovic speaking, and he says: "I wish to know why isn't the commission for electing and appointing getting other materials. I personally have problems in Trebinje, for it has been three to four months since we have sent proposals for electing judges, and we were explained that those papers were lost somewhere in the ministry." And at the bottom of his speech, which is on the next page in the B/C/S, he says: "I wish to ask Minister Rosic, do you know if the acts which were sent from down there were arrived? Were they sent in the legally regular manner," et cetera. And then you reply and you say: "We have several objections that the propositions of certain municipalities, parties and companies are being withheld for a long time. However, I can say that the government is not keeping any acts, but is sending them to the party. From the moment the party started working, and immediately after they come from the party, they are being sent to the first government session to come." And then you say: "I really do not know why certain proposals did not pass through." Now, what you were saying here, Dr. Lukic, is that -- you're explaining the government's delay in acting on certain municipality proposals, and the reason for that delay was that these proposals were being sent to the SDS and approved by the -- and had to be approved by the SDS before they could be addressed at a government session. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: You know, you're asking me about something that is written here, whether I said it and why I said it. Now, I probably did say it, because it's written here, but when was it? I have to tell you that as for the correspondents -- well, the names mentioned are familiar to me. But what was said on that occasion or what was not said, at any rate, what I see is that you -- your drift is the SDS. I wasn't in the SDS when Dr. Karadzic appointed me prime minister designate. Therefore, in my firm view, the SDS was not against the government or Republika Srpska. It asked that its views be taken into consideration and that it, too, participate in this ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, but you're not answering my question. My question was for you to confirm that what you said in this speech was in effect the reason for the delay in certain -- in government action on certain municipality proposals was because those proposals had to be sent first to the SDS for their approval before they could be addressed at a government session. That's what you're saying here; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Not always, and not at any cost. I will tell you that some of the SDS members from Banja Luka sent a proposal to the government for 23 managers or directors to be removed, and we told them that they had to first discuss the matter at the Municipal Assembly and that only then could we remove them from office. And what came back to us as a result of that was only a request for one of these directors to be removed. So you seem to be driving hard against the SDS, targeting the SDS far too harshly as if the SDS had come from a different state.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to another topic now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could have P3106, and this is the exhibit discussed at paragraph 19. It's the 61st government session on the 21st of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is the government session, Dr. Lukic, where the leadership of the government was handed over from Branko Djeric to you. And in your statement you said with respect to this session: "I insisted that all property acquired by illegal means must be returned to its owners regardless of ethnicity." And if we could go to page 4 of this document. And this is in the middle of the page. And what you actually said as reflected in these minutes, and this is the third paragraph from the bottom in the English: "All measures should be taken in order to return illegally obtained properties to their owners, i.e., to government bodies if ownership cannot be proven." And, in fact, Dr. Lukic, throughout your tenure as prime minister, you repeated emphasized the importance of collecting illegally obtained property at the republic level and placing it in the state coffers. So in other words, your concern about stolen property was not to return it to their owners but to collect it and use it to fund the state; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: God forbid. As a man of the profession that I belong to, I could never espouse a principle which would take someone's property away from him. I am aware of the fact that property can be acquired by way of three means and whoever is an owner of property could have come by that property only through these three ways. I have always advocated such views in the government, when talking to Dr. Karadzic and many others, and have always in this been supported. In this civil war of ours, there was only the case of temporarily seizing the property of someone so that it can be preserved during the war, but as for this, this sort of behaviour, wherever I appeared as a member of the government, this was all rejected. For instance, I came to Banja Luka and there was a man who took for himself somebody else's house and then also took away somebody else's flat for his daughter and another for his son. None of the municipal bodies approved this, but, you see, people were doing this contrary to what that -- the official position was. You see, I do come from that profession. I know what property means and how it is acquired and how it can be protected. There were such times where we said that nobody can be allowed to stay out in the street where there is rain or snow, even if we have to take a flat belonging to a Serb, Jew, Croat, Muslim, et cetera, but not in such a way so as to drive these people out of their properties but merely to save others, to save their lives. And now we see this policy that was present from day one, that very many people, our citizens, regardless of their ethnicity, did repossess their property.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at P3129, which is an associated exhibit, at paragraph 33. This is the 66th government session from the 20th of March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: On the first page you can see under the agenda, item 2 is report on the financing problems in the Army of Republika Srpska. And if we could go to page 3 in the English and page 5 in the B/C/S. This is the discussion under that item of financing problems in the VRS, and it says that: "Concrete measures were proposed at the meeting," this is about halfway down the paragraph, "with emphasis on the fact that," and this is at the next page in the English, "attention must be paid to the consistent implementation of the adopted regulations, particularly those concerning war booty and illegally obtained property." And then it says: "The government assessed the focus of activities and measures should be primarily on the following." And further down the page in the English and on page 6 in the B/C/S under number 4, it says: "Place all war booty from material assets to money and foreign currency considered socially owned property under the control of the state. Material assets and money seized from war profiteers and money earned in unlawful and illegal ways is to be placed under the control of the state and used for the defence of the republic." Dr. Lukic, these minutes reflect the efforts of your government to collect unlawfully obtained money and property and use it to finance the army; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: A moment ago I felt that you did not say quite properly that we had national wealth such as forests, et cetera, and that we transformed it into state property. Secondly, we tried that all the items considered to be war booty be placed at the disposal of the general public good, especially for the defence of the country, the army, et cetera. When it comes to unlawfully obtained property, misappropriated, stolen, et cetera, I have to tell you that the struggle on that front is still going on and is far from over. So this is something that is still pending.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Lukic, I'm going to press you a little on this because these minutes don't reflect any kind of struggle -- please listen to my question.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: These minutes do not reflect any kind of struggle against unlawfully obtaining property. They say quite clearly that unlawfully obtained property is to be placed under the control of the state and used for the defence of the republic. In other words, this isn't about countering crime, this is about benefiting from crime, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: This wasn't something the government did at all. It had its bodies, and it assigned tasks to them. Accordingly, one knew exactly which of these assignments were given to which of these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P3141 now. This is an associated exhibit discussed at paragraph 61, and they are the minutes of the 82nd government session from September and October 1993, and we can see that Dr. Karadzic and other members of the state leadership were in attendance. And if we could go to page 12 of the English and page 13 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Under item 42, number 2, it says: "It was concluded that all goods treated as war booty and which was obtained illegally which is presently in the possession of the Ministry of the Interior shall be given to the republican commodity reserves." And two government ministers are tasked with implementing this decision. This is another reflection of the government's efforts to collect for its own benefit unlawfully acquired property, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: No. Firstly, the property was acquired regularly and lawfully by the government in our view and was handed over to those bodies that would use it in the best possible way for the purposes of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, whether or not you viewed your acquisition and use of this property as lawful and appropriate, the property was initially obtained illegally. That's what these minutes state; right? This was stolen property, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Why would it constitute a mistake that the government should make sure that the unlawfully acquired property is given over for the purposes of the general good?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me ask you about the war profiteering that occurred in the government prior to yours. Now, it's right, isn't it, that both Mico Stanisic and Momcilo Mandic, two ministers in the government before yours, were involved in the appropriation and sale of Golf vehicles from the TAS factory; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that there were stories of that kind, but they were never proven. To put it simply, those bodies that investigated such stories did not collect enough hard evidence in order to prosecute anybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 25027, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this document is a report from August 1996 from the Main Staff counter-intelligence group reporting on a conversation with you on the 1st of August, 1996. Oh, I see we're still waiting for the B/C/S. While we're waiting, Dr. Lukic, maybe I can start by asking you some general questions. The first part of this report relates that you had attacked the VRS for essentially betraying the Krajina. Do you recall expressing the view around this time that you were angry at the VRS for its failure to prevent the fall of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I cannot read this, nor can I see when I stated anything like that. Of course I am angry because of the fall of the RSK, but this whole text isn't like my way of communicating at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes. And I apologise. We're having some troubles getting the B/C/S on the screen, so I'll try to make my questions clear nevertheless. This relates to a conversation with you on the 1st of August, 1996, and this would have been with an intelligence operative of the VRS, although you may not have been aware of that person's status. It's unclear. And on page 2, in the second full paragraph, it says that you were cautioned by the person you were speaking to that you were also a member of the Supreme Command and knew everything that was taking place and had never prevented war profiteering and robbery, and that the commission investigating the Golf affair never even started working. You are reported to have replied: "I was going to help Koljevic because he was the commission's president, but the services failed to do their part of the job. I know it was on Radovan's orders that Mico Stanisic was selling the Golfs, that Jovo Tintor and Mirko Krajisnik were selling, that Momo Mandic was selling and now he is the director of the Sarajevska Banka in Belgrade. But again I can -- this was never seen before, the army fleeing in front of the people." Now, that's right, isn't it, on -- in August of 1996, you stated that Momo Mandic and Mico Stanisic, among others, were selling the Golfs and that they were doing so on Radovan's orders; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that you took the year 1996, which is not relevant for some relations as at the time when I was prime minister. That's one thing. And I remember exactly -- I remember my very words, that it is unheard in the history of the Serbian people that the army fled before the people. And I have nothing to add or subtract there. And as for the Golfs and other things, well, you mentioned Stanisic, Mandic, Tintor and others, it is true that they were involved in some dealings with all that, and it's true that the leaders of the republic knew about some things, but any other stories remain unproven. So it cannot be the object of discussion in the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. I believe that this issue regarding the Golfs, number one, is irrelevant and when it involves Dr. Karadzic it becomes prejudicial; and secondly, I don't believe that the witness has confirmed anything about his conversation with this operative other than the fact that he recalled saying that he'd never seen the army fleeing in front of the people, which I don't think is significant for the Prosecution as far as admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I disagree on both counts. The witness has essentially confirmed the contents of the document, not just the actions of the VRS, but he said: "And as for the Golfs and other things, well, you mentioned Stanisic, Mandic, Tintor and others, it is true that they were involved in some dealings with all that, and it is true that the leaders of the republic knew about some things, but ... other stories remain unproven." So it's certainly a confirmation of the essence of the conversation, and in terms of the relevance, I think it's highly relevant that the minister of justice and minister of the interior in 1992 were involved in war profiteering activities and certainly with the -- and certainly any knowledge or an acquiescence on the part of the accused would be relevant given the Defence position that this was a state struggling to impose the rule of law in chaotic circumstances. So I don't think the objection is well founded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Let's say it were true that Dr. Karadzic was somehow involved in Golfs or some thefts of Golfs, which he denies, but let's say that that were true. How would that be relevant to what he's being prosecuted for here, a joint criminal enterprise to expel Muslims from Serb-controlled areas. And it's highly prejudicial to -- to introduce evidence of this kind of theft or dishonesty in a trial. And secondly, the document, the portion of the document that the Prosecution wants to use, that somehow this was on Dr. Karadzic's orders, is not confirmed at all by the witness. So I don't think that this is either a topic or a document that is relevant, and it shouldn't be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I contribute to the clarification? Where was it established that these people sold all these for their own needs? They are ministers and the state has the right sell its own property. How was the assertion that they were war profiteers founded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. We are dealing with admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By majority, Judge Baird dissenting, the Chamber will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6341, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic, I'd like to move on to another topic, and the next document I'll be using is P783. At paragraph 5 of your statement, you say that in 1991, Professor Koljevic invited you to give Dr. Karadzic your opinion on the best route for linking up the Krajina with Semberija, and that you told Dr. Karadzic that the only link was through the valley along the Sava and that the road across Majevica was only a last resort. When in 1991 was this meeting you had with Dr. Karadzic, roughly?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: It was in the autumn of 1991. I said that the best way that leads through a valley was the one along the right bank of the Sava, and that is the truth. That's when I first met Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Could we zoom in on the top part of the map. That's good.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Lukic, the usher will assist you with the pen, and I'd like you to please draw that link between Krajina and Semberija through the Sava River valley that you proposed to Dr. Karadzic in 1991.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: This is it. This isn't very precise. I apologise. But along the right bank of the Sava, of course wherever you could go through. And this is the right way in all weather conditions, and it is the easiest to defend.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you just mentioned that it is the easiest to defend, which brings me to my next question, which is that in 1991 when you had this conversation, of course these areas were all linked because they were all within the Bosnian entity, which was at that time a whole entity, indeed part of Yugoslavia. So when you were proposing a route for linking these areas in 1991, this must have been a proposal as to how these entities could be linked together in some future separate Bosnian Serb entity. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: No, because this was not considered at the time. The only consideration was for the large number of inhabitants of Bosanska Krajina to be linked by an appropriate route for economic, medical, and other reasons. You know very well that the -- in Banja Luka, 12 babies died because there wasn't enough oxygen. It couldn't be brought there because that route had been cut. It was a way of linking the west and the east of what's today Republika Srpska, and further on to Serbia, in order to make possible supply, the supply of such material as was in short supply in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know why you're asking this question given that this was in late 1991 and our enemies already had their units established, and we have -- we had already seen how events would unfold.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you talked about babies dying in Banja Luka with -- because there wasn't enough oxygen and it couldn't be brought there. That was something that happened during the war when those areas were less accessible. But in 1991, when you suggested this route to Dr. Karadzic, there was no problem traversing from the Krajina to Semberija; right? There were roads connecting all these locations. The only reason you could be proposing a link between these areas is if you were contemplating a separate Serb entity; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: No. It was to too early for such contemplations. You probably don't know that in the inner part of Posavina there was a total disruption of communication between the west and the east of today's Republika Srpska or Bosnia-Herzegovina. That problem with communication had started much earlier, and it made us all think about how one day we can solve that communication problem and be linked to the others. And I believe that it is clear to you that since the Croatian side and the Muslim side had established their forces much earlier, we were already -- we already had fears that this communication problem would cost us many lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Could we go to P3474, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were you going to tender that marked map?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I was, and then it disappeared, so I wasn't going to bother with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's kept, albeit without signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If it's kept, then I would like to tender it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6342, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. This, Dr. Lukic, is an article from February 1992 from "Derventski List," and it's titled "Bridge to the Krajinas." And on the first page, the first paragraph on the very upper left-hand side in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it's legible --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yeah, we'll have to zoom in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- for Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Zoom in quite a bit on the very upper left-hand corner. And it's the first paragraph of text after the bolded text at the top. And it's -- reports on a meeting held in Doboj by the SDS Executive Committee -- sorry, a meeting about the SDS Executive Committee reporting on a Doboj meeting attended by representatives of the autonomous districts in the area as well as Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and Vojislav Maksimovic. And if we could go to the top of the second column in B/C/S and the next page in the English. It says that serious consideration was given to the necessity to establish communication and geographical links, and it talks about Northern Bosnia being a bridge and a natural line between the two Krajinas, the Knin and the Bosanska Krajina, and Semberija and Serbia on the other side. And then in the third paragraph on that page it says: "The part of the Republic of Croatia settled by Serbian people exactly opposite Northern Bosnia along the Okucani-Virovitica line constitutes an almost identical bridge between areas containing Croatian populations. For this reason, guided by these ethnic and geographical facts, in Doboj the idea of transferring the Moslavina Serbs to Northern Bosnia and transferring the Croats from Northern Bosnia to the areas along the Okucani-Virovitica line in exchange was publicly advanced for the first time."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, this proposal of transferring Croats from Northern Bosnia to Croatia in exchange for Serbs from Croatia, this relates to that same area that you proposed to Dr. Karadzic as a link between Krajina and Semberija; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. This can't be allowed. Why call this a proposal? If anybody mentioned this then -- or if anybody proposed this, then we -- Ms. Gustafson should say if it was accepted. So it was not proposed. It was merely mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you answer the question, Dr. Lukic? This area they're talking about, an idea of transferring --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I haven't read this before. I didn't know about this article. But if you want to speak about the connection between eastern and Western Bosnia again, or the Krajinas and Semberija, or maybe the eastern part of the RS and Serbia, that's what I have already explained. This will remain unchanged. And as for this resettling, I have never read about this before, and nobody made such a proposal to me ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Could we go to 65 ter 24995, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Dr. Lukic, the document that's about to appear, that I see has appeared now, is an interview with you in the magazine "Srpska Vojska," the official VRS publication, dated the 20th of May, 1993. Do you recall giving an interview to "Srpska Vojska" around this time?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: If it says here, I probably did, but I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. On the first page, in the second paragraph, and this is towards the bottom of the far left-hand column in the B/C/S, you were asked about the Vance-Owen Plan, and you say: "The Vance-Owen maps are so bad for the Serbian people that it is really very difficult to talk about them. They are unacceptable primarily from the point of departure that they have split up the Serbian region. Through the Posavina province which they given to the Croats, they have cut us off from Krajina and turned it into Nagorno-Karabakh. This is a cul-de-sac. The corridor is practically just a controlled road." Now, here you are criticising the Vance-Owen Plan because it did not provide for a sufficiently wide corridor link between the Krajina and other Serb-held territories; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I must tell you one thing here. Your Honours, I was against the Vance-Owen Plan. At the Assembly at Jahorina of which you certainly know, two years ago I undertook to study the Vance-Owen Plan again, and the result was that -- my repeated conclusion that I was right. I would be against the Vance-Owen Plan even today. So there's no point in asking me anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'd like to ask you one more thing about it which is --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but now that you were reading, I noticed that I indeed stated this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2 of the B/C/S and the middle column towards the bottom -- sorry, page 2 of the English and the middle column towards the bottom on page 1 of the B/C/S. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
